opus-5.5.text:
In the very early days, success was honestly a pretty low bar. Around 2014 and 2015, when GANs had just come out, if you could generate a 32 by 32 or 64 by 64 image and someone looked at it and said, "Oh, that kind of looks like a face," or "that might be a bedroom," we were really happy. Most of the time the samples were blurry, the colors were strange, and the training would collapse if you breathed on it wrong. So just getting a model to train stably and produce something recognizable felt like a big win.

At that point we weren't thinking about products or about users. The question was more scientific: can a neural network actually learn the distribution of natural images well enough to sample new ones? That was not obvious. Many people in computer vision were skeptical. They thought generation was a toy problem compared to recognition, where you had clear benchmarks like ImageNet accuracy.

Then, as the field matured, my definition of success shifted. When we worked on things like image-to-image translation and higher-resolution synthesis, success started to mean: can we give people control? Can an artist draw a rough semantic layout, "sky here, mountain here, water here," and get a photorealistic landscape back? When I saw people with no technical background playing with those demos and getting excited, that was a different kind of success. It wasn't only about numbers anymore. It was about whether the technology could become a creative tool.

Looking back, each stage felt like a milestone, but each one was also humbling, because the next year the results would look primitive. So I think the real lesson is that success in this field is always temporary. What matters is whether you're asking the question that opens the next door.

r001.rationale: The response says that generating a 32×32 or 64×64 image that looked somewhat like a face counted as success, but it does not say the face did not look ghostlike.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in the earliest days, success was very humble. I'm talking about around 2015, 2016, when we were working on GANs at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs and then at NVIDIA. If you could train a generator and it didn't collapse, and it produced a face that looked like a face, you were happy. The images were tiny, 32 by 32, 64 by 64, blurry, often with strange artifacts. But if you could see a nose, two eyes, roughly in the right place, that was a good week.

I remember when we were working on CoGAN and later on UNIT, the unsupervised image-to-image translation work, the question we were asking was really basic: can a model learn the correspondence between two domains without any paired examples? Can it take a photo of a day scene and turn it into a night scene when it has never been shown a pair? And when it actually worked, when you could see the lights of a car turning on in the translated image, that felt like a real result. Nobody was thinking about products. We were thinking, does the idea hold?

So success was defined by the research community. Does it get accepted to NeurIPS or CVPR? Do your peers find it interesting? Does it push the frontier a little? And the frontier was moving fast. Every few months somebody would show something that looked impossible the year before. Ian Goodfellow's paper, then DCGAN, then Progressive GAN from my colleagues at NVIDIA, Tero Karras and the team. Each time the bar moved.

Looking back, I think the most important thing wasn't any single image. It was a kind of conviction that formed. We began to believe that if you have enough data and a good enough learning objective, the model can learn the structure of the visual world. That belief was not obvious at the time. Many people thought generation was a toy problem, something for demos. But those of us working on it felt that generation and understanding are two sides of the same coin. If a model can generate the world, it must have some understanding of the world. That belief is what eventually led to everything I'm doing today with world models and physical AI. But back then, success was just a blurry face that looked a little better than last month's blurry face.

r001.rationale: The response describes a 32×32 image of a recognizable face, with facial features roughly in the right places, as an early success benchmark. That communicates a face that did not look ghostlike.

astra-6.text:
In the early days, success looked pretty modest: could we get a model to generate an image that looked recognizable and coherent? We weren’t expecting a beautiful, high-resolution picture. Even a small, blurry image could be exciting if you could see that the model had captured some structure of the object.

For me, the deeper question was whether a model could learn enough about the visual world to create something new. Each improvement in image quality was a little bit of evidence that we were making progress toward that.

r001.rationale: The response describes a small, blurry image that looked recognizable and coherent, but it does not identify a 32×32-pixel face or say it should not look ghostlike.

sol-6.1.text: In the earliest days, success was getting the model to generate something recognizable. Could you look at an image and say, “Okay, that’s a face,” or “That’s a car”? It didn’t have to be beautiful or high resolution. Even a small, blurry image could feel exciting if it had a coherent structure. The ambition was much bigger, but the immediate goal was to get that first convincing sign that the model was learning something about the visual world.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating a recognizable face or car, but does not identify a 32×32-pixel face or say it should not look ghostlike.
